new_statements.quote: Una palabra fonémica (grupo acentual) en este dialecto del Orejón, generalmente se marca con el acento primario inicial en la raíz gramatical (la raíz siempre es inicial en una palabra fonológica). Este acento primario se encuentra en todas las sílabas de la raíz si las sílabas tienen tonos idénticos. Pero si los tonos no son idénticos, solamente las sílabas de tono alto se acentúan. Todas las raíces monosilábicas tienen el acento primario. [...] Los acentos primario y secundario, iniciales en una palabra fonológica, son de esta manera fonémicos, ya que su ubicación es predecible sólo gramaticalmente, aunque no estén escritos en este trabajo. [p. 9, sec. 2.1.1:] Hay dos tonos contrastivos en el Orejón: alto /´/ y bajo / / (no diacrítico).
new_statements.translation: A phonemic word (accentual group) in this dialect of Orejón is generally marked with primary accent initial on the grammatical root (the root is always initial in a phonological word). This primary accent is found on all syllables of the root if the syllables have identical tones. But if the tones are not identical, only the high-tone syllables are accented. All monosyllabic roots carry primary accent. [...] The primary and secondary accents, initial in a phonological word, are in this way phonemic, since their location is predictable only grammatically, although they are not written in this work. [p. 9:] There are two contrastive tones in Orejón: high /´/ and low (no diacritic).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for orej1242 has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this source supplies the first placement statement: a two-tone language with grammatically predictable root(-initial) primary accent conditioned by root tone, plus rhythmic secondary accent on suffixes. Nothing in the catalog is contradicted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Orejón has two contrastive lexical tones (high, low), demonstrated with minimal pairs and root tone patterns (HH, HL, LL; LHL, HHL, HLL, LLL on trisyllables). Word accent is separate from tone and morphologically placed: primary accent falls on the root, which is always word-initial; within a polysyllabic root every syllable is accented if the root's tones are all identical, otherwise only the high-toned root syllables are accented; monosyllabic roots always bear primary accent. Accent placement is predictable from grammatical structure (root position), not lexically contrastive, and the authors do not write it. Intonation starts high and declines through the phonological word; word boundaries are cued by primary accent plus a pitch reset.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary accent falls on the first syllable of a polysyllabic suffix string immediately after the root and then on alternate syllables of the following suffixes in a regular predictable pattern (examples /ʔi"hína?/ 'todos los gusanos', /hĩgo"húna?/ 'todas las palomas', with " marking secondary accent); it weakens progressively toward the end of the phonological word. Footnote 7 adds morphotonemic rules: all suffixes are underlyingly low; the first syllable of a suffix string becomes high; if the string has only two syllables the second is also high when open; a single monosyllabic suffix copies the tone of the root-final syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Roots with non-identical tones: only the high-toned syllables take primary accent (so an LH(L) root has non-initial primary accent within the root). Four-syllable forms are compounds of two or more roots and 'there may be other primary accents inside the word'. Contrastive interrogative intonation patterns noted but deferred to a future grammar. Description is of the Esperanza (Loreto) dialect, ~50 speakers; Sucusari, Yanayacu and Algodón river dialect variants are mentioned only for segmental allophony ([tš] of /s/, [gw]~[ʔu], [y]~[dž]), not for accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Velie, Brend & Powlison 1976 describe the Orejón dialect spoken by about fifty people at Esperanza, Loreto, Peru (data collected by Velie 1958-1960); variants from the Sucusari, Yanayacu and Algodón river dialects are cited only for segmental allophones. The language is the one now called Máíhɨ̃kì/Maihiki (orej1242); the paper uses the exonym Orejón (also 'coto' in the 1975 title).

tone_statements.citation: Skilton, Amalia. 2014. The Northern/Putumayo Basin dialect of Máíhɨ̃kì: A field report. Unpublished ms., UC Berkeley, 36 pp. (Glottolog ref 577317; likely in CLA deposit 'Materials of the Berkeley Maihiki Project', doi:10.7297/X2DR2SGD)
tone_statements.quote: In the Napo varieties of Máı́hı̃ki, according to our current analysis, H tone always spreads from an HH verb root or an intrinsically HH verbal suffix to an immediately following present tense (for all verbs) and past tense (for regular-class verbs) declarative inflectional suffix. Tone spreading of this type is absent from NM: HH verbs do not spread the root’s H tone to finite inflectional suffixes. Rather, the inflectional suffix surfaces as L due to the language’s Align-L(HL,PrWd) constraint. This pattern holds for both regular- and ni-class verbs.
tone_statements.locator: p. 11, sec. 3.1 'Prosodic behavior of finite verbal inflection' (p. 11)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Dialect report assuming an H/L tone analysis (root classes HH, HL, LL); no inventory statement or tone count given; only 'phonetic downdrift' of H mentioned; roots subject to a bimoraic constraint.

tone_statements.quote: Cada vocal oral y cada vocal nasal también lleva un tono alto o un tono bajo. El tono alto señalamos con un tilde de acento agudo (´) y el tono bajo señalamos con un tilde de acento grave ( `). ... Las palabras se distinguen por tener vocales nasales en vez de vocales orales y por tener tono alto en vez de tono bajo. ... El Cuadro 2 abajo, por ejemplo, muestra cuatro pares de palabras que solamente se distinguen por las diferencias en los tonos de las vocales. Hay cientos de ejemplos más de palabras que se distinguen solamente por su tono.
tone_statements.translation: Each oral vowel and each nasal vowel also carries a high tone or a low tone. We mark the high tone with an acute accent (´) and the low tone with a grave accent (`). ... Words are distinguished by having nasal vowels instead of oral vowels and by having high tone instead of low tone. ... Table 2 below, for example, shows four pairs of words that are distinguished only by differences in the tones of the vowels. There are hundreds more examples of words distinguished solely by their tone.
tone_statements.summary: Two tones, H (acute) and L (grave), on every vowel; Cuadro 2 actually prints two minimal pairs (násó/nàsò, dóáyí/dòàyì); classifiers and some bound morphemes are toneless, taking tone from neighbours (fn. 2, sec. 0.5.3). forms_shown is 'at least'.

tone_statements.quote: This paper will argue that Máíjɨqui (formerly Orejón or Coto)1, an endangered Western Tukanoan language of the Northern Peruvian Amazon basin, has developed a tone system that differs from those of its family members in that it is both privative and equipollent (i.e., that it has phonologically active H and L tone plus a third value that is analyzed as null). ... My analysis of the prosodic system of Máíjɨqui includes spreading H tone, L tone (derived from loss of glottal stop), and a null tone that is assigned a default low pitch.
tone_statements.summary: Three-way underlying contrast H / L / Ø (source counts null as 'a third tonal category'); author calls it 'both privative and equipollent'. Word prominence = high pitch; source never says 'stress'.

In: Reports year 1, 2013-02.086, "Materials of the Berkeley Máíhɨ̃kì Project", California Language Archive, Survey of California and Other Indian Languages, University of California, Berkeley. doi:10.7297/X28913VZ
tone_statements.quote: All verb roots in MAIh#ki have an inherent tone pattern. So far, we believe that there are three patterns: a HH pattern, a LL pattern and a HL pattern. ... When it comes to tone in MAIh#ki, there are four kinds of morphemes. The first is the root, which bears immutable H or L tones ... The second kind of morpheme is the 'tone-switching' Class 1 affix, which, when it appears directly following the verb root, takes the opposite tone of the verb root. ... Monosyllabic nouns may be either high or low. Disyllabic monomorphemic nouns may be HH, HL or LL.
tone_statements.locator: unpaginated ODT: section 'Tone > Verbs', 'Analysis' and 'Tone on Nouns'
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones H/L; roots have fixed patterns (HH, HL, LL; LH doubtful); suffixes toneless-polar, always-H, or copy preceding tone. Test frame: prohibitive -bai. ASCII transcription; 60+ forms.

tone_statements.citation: Bellier, Irène (1986). La part des femmes: essai sur les rapports entre les femmes et les hommes mai huna, Amazonie péruvienne, I-II-III. Thèse de doctorat. París: EHESS.
tone_statements.quote: Nous n'avons pas noté tous les tons, dont l'existence semble certaine mais qui n'ont pas été étudiés et que nous distinguions difficilement de l'intonation propre au contexte grammatical. Nous les indiquons dans les cas de redoublement de voyelles, dans les onomatopées, ou lorsque nous sommes certaine de leurs réalisations. ... Ils réintroduisaient notamment les distinctions morphématiques et sémantiques liées au système des tons et rétablissaient les syllabes qui ont tendance à tomber en fin de mot...
tone_statements.translation: We have not marked all the tones, whose existence seems certain but which have not been studied and which we had difficulty distinguishing from the intonation proper to the grammatical context. We indicate them in cases of vowel doubling, in onomatopoeia, or when we are certain of their realisation. ... They [the consultants] notably reintroduced the morphemic and semantic distinctions linked to the tone system and restored the syllables that tend to drop at the end of the word...
tone_statements.locator: vol. 1 p. 17, 'Note sur la transcription de la langue mai huna'
tone_statements.summary: Ethnographic thesis: tones said to exist but unstudied, no inventory. Vol. 2 p. 403 fn 19: 'L'accent tonal permet de distinger.. mɨ̀ɨ̀bɨ hã.. mɨ́ɨ́bɨ̃ ha' (grave vs acute on the page).

readall_conflicts: No new source was opened, so no new disagreement can be established. The only known tension is second-hand: the two SIL works (Velie 1975: 12-13; Velie et al. 1976: 11-12) speak of 'acento' in Orejón, which the catalog's deciding source (Farmer & Michael 2013 ms, fn. 19, p. 35) judges 'does not correspond to the modern understanding of stress'; whether the SIL 'acento' is a stress rule (e.g. a fixed-position prominence) or a notation for the H tone cannot be checked until SIL entry 30074) or the DEL 10 sketch is obtained through a browser or a library.

audit.reasoning: The 'tonal, no word stress' coding rests on the two best available first-hand descriptions: Farmer's 2015 Berkeley dissertation (phonology chapter, all three dialects) and the dedicated Farmer & Michael 2013 tone manuscript, which states twice that there is no evidence of stress, contrasts Máíhɨ̃kì explicitly with mixed stress-tone Eastern Tukanoan systems, and settles the older SIL 'accent' notation. Both quotations were confirmed verbatim at the cited pages in held PDFs. No later published version, instrumental study, or competing analysis was found (Michael's 2021 CV; Skilton 2017 downloaded and silent on prosody). Remaining unheld items (Skilton 2014 NM field report; Velie 1975/1976 SIL sketches) are low-priority and unlikely to alter the classification.

tone.quote: In the Napo varieties of Máı́hı̃ki, according to our current analysis, H tone always spreads from an HH verb root or an intrinsically HH verbal suffix to an immediately following present tense (for all verbs) and past tense (for regular-class verbs) declarative inflectional suffix. Tone spreading of this type is absent from NM: HH verbs do not spread the root’s H tone to finite inflectional suffixes. Rather, the inflectional suffix surfaces as L due to the language’s Align-L(HL,PrWd) constraint. This pattern holds for both regular- and ni-class verbs.

tone.quote: Nous n'avons pas noté tous les tons, dont l'existence semble certaine mais qui n'ont pas été étudiés et que nous distinguions difficilement de l'intonation propre au contexte grammatical. Nous les indiquons dans les cas de redoublement de voyelles, dans les onomatopées, ou lorsque nous sommes certaine de leurs réalisations. ... Ils réintroduisaient notamment les distinctions morphématiques et sémantiques liées au système des tons et rétablissaient les syllabes qui ont tendance à tomber en fin de mot...
tone.locator: vol. 1 p. 17, 'Note sur la transcription de la langue mai huna'
tone.translation: We have not marked all the tones, whose existence seems certain but which have not been studied and which we had difficulty distinguishing from the intonation proper to the grammatical context. We indicate them in cases of vowel doubling, in onomatopoeia, or when we are certain of their realisation. ... They [the consultants] notably reintroduced the morphemic and semantic distinctions linked to the tone system and restored the syllables that tend to drop at the end of the word...
